newsitem.title: GERMANY: Hoechst readies HMR for possible float.
newsitem.headline: Hoechst readies HMR for possible float.

text.p: Germany's Hoechst AG on Wednesday removed a key obstacle to the flotation of its drugs unit Hoechst Marion Roussel but also signalled that a listing may no longer be its first choice for the unit.
In a widely anticipated step, Europe's largest chemicals group will buy the 43.3 percent stake in French drugs group Roussel Uclaf SA it does not own for 18.1 billion francs or 5.3 billion marks.

Analysts said the price, while relatively high, is affordable, especially after Hoechst on Tuesday said it would remove about four billion marks in debt by selling its specialty chemicals business to Swiss group Clariant AG.
"I expect they will be able to finance this with loans and that there will be no need for a capital increase," said Markus Rausch, analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Frankfurt.

By acquiring the stake Hoechst will now be able to turn its drugs unit HMR, which takes the name from the three partners Hoechst, U.S. group Marion Merrell Down and Roussel Uclaf, into a separate legal entity, a preconditon for listing the group.
Overall analysts agreed the move is a smart step, putting Hoechst in an even better position to improve its ranking as a leading drugs group.

While Hoechst, one of Germany's most vocal supporters of boosting shareholder value, has long hinted it may float HMR shares, industry sources say preferences may have changed as management may be mulling alternative strategies.

Stressing there is no direct tie-in between Hoechst's plan to buy the Roussel stake and a bourse listing for HMR, Hoechst chief financial officer Klaus Schmieder told a news conference in Paris that no final decision has been made on a flotation.
"The listing of HMR is an issue. We are contemplating doing that, but we have not made a decision yet."

Analysts said Schmieder's remarks hinted Hoechst may be moving away from this idea, which to them had appeared to be definite and scheduled for late 1997, some time after the listing of Hoechst AG shares in the U.S. was completed.
"It sounds like Hoechst is taking a step back on the plan," said Peter Blair, analyst at Salomon Brothers in London.
A Hoechst spokesman however stressed the group had always said an HMR listing was merely one option, not a firm plan.
Industry sources said there may now be two competing schools of thought but that a decision on the course of action will be taken before the May, 1997 annual meeting.

In a bid to improve transparency, Hoechst may choose to list the HMR drugs unit next year in Frankfurt, New York, and Paris and list its AgrEvo crop-protection joint venture, run with German drugs group Schering AG, in 1999, sources said.

A competing plan however may be for Hoechst to spin off more of its vast chemicals activities, thereby tailoring itself largely into a life-sciences group with drugs, agriculture and diagnostic activities.
As Hoechst AG shares are already listed, this option would avoid the need to list HMR and AgrEvo separately.
"If everything else is spun off, then Hoechst would be a very transparent group and the need to list other units would be gone," a source said.

Salomon's Blair said it would be logical to wonder if this is becoming the preferred scenario, especially in light of a thorny tax issue seen to complicate a possible HMR listing. "Maybe one way to avoid the tax issue may be not to list HMR."

Analysts agreed that Hoechst's management is dynamic and capable of firing off still more surprises, including another possible big merger in the pharmaceuticals area at a time the industry is still going through heavy consolidation.
The Swiss mega-merger of Ciba Geigy AG and Sandoz AG into Norvatis AG has fuelled many companies' imaginations and unleashed a steady stream of rumours about possible mergers.

Turning to talk that France's remaining large drugs groups Rhone Poulenc SA, Sanofi SA, and Synthelabo SA, a unit of L'Oreal SA may be planning a super merger in the wake of the Hoechst deal, Salomon's Blair said, "I would not write anything off."
